Rules:

1	Legal Consequences of Rescheduling
     2	Marijuana
     3	Updated May 1, 2024
     4	On April 30, 2024, news outlets reported that the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) planned to
     5	move marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). The
     6	planned
     7	change followed an August 2023 recommendation from the Department of Health and Human Services
     8	(HHS) that DEA reschedule marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III. Any change to the status of
     9	marijuana via the DEA rulemaking process would not take effect immediately. According to reports,
    10	the
    11	proposal will be reviewed by the White House Office of Management and Budget and will then be
    12	subject
    13	to public comment.
    14	A previous CRS Insight outlined policy considerations related to rescheduling marijuana. This Legal
    15	Sidebar provides additional information on the legal consequences of the possible move of marijuana
    16	from Schedule I to Schedule III.
    17	Current Legal Status of Cannabis Under the CSA
    18	Cannabis and its derivatives generally fall within one of two categories under federal law:
    19	marijuana or
    20	hemp. Unless an exception applies, the CSA classifies the cannabis plant and its derivatives as
    21	marijuana
    22	(some provisions of the statute use an alternative spelling, “marihuana”). The CSA definition of
    23	marijuana excludes (1) products that meet the legal definition of hemp and (2) the mature stalks of
    24	the
    25	cannabis plant; the sterilized seeds of the plant; and fibers, oils, and other products made from
    26	the stalks
    27	and seeds. Marijuana is a Schedule I controlled substance under the CSA.
    28	Federal law defines hemp as the cannabis plant or any part of that plant with a delta-9
    29	tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration of no more than 0.3%. The non-psychoactive compound
    30	cannabidiol (CBD) falls within the legal definition of hemp. Hemp is not a controlled substance
    31	under the
    32	CSA.
    33	Substances become subject to the CSA through placement in one of five lists, known as Schedules I
    34	through V. Congress placed marijuana in Schedule I in 1970 when it enacted the CSA. A lower schedule
    35	number carries greater restrictions under the CSA, with controlled substances in Schedule I subject
    36	to the
    37	most stringent controls. Schedule I controlled substances have no currently accepted medical use. It
    38	is
    39	illegal to produce, dispense, or possess such substances except in the context of federally approved
    40	Congressional Research Service
    41	https://crsreports.congress.gov
    42	LSB11105
    43	Congressional Research Service 2
    44	scientific studies, subject to CSA regulatory requirements designed to prevent abuse and diversion.
    45	Unauthorized activities involving Schedule I controlled substances are federal crimes that may give
    46	rise to
    47	large fines and significant jail time. DEA is required to set annual production quotas for Schedule
    48	I
    49	controlled substances manufactured for use in approved research.
    50	In addition to the general regulatory framework that applies due to marijuana’s Schedule I status,
    51	some
    52	provisions of the CSA apply specifically to marijuana. For instance, 21 U.S.C. § 841 imposes
    53	mandatory
    54	minimum prison sentences for persons convicted of criminal CSA violations involving set quantities
    55	of
    56	specific controlled substances, including marijuana. In addition, 21 U.S.C. § 823 creates special
    57	registration requirements for those who manufacture marijuana for research purposes.
    58	In sharp contrast to the stringent federal control of marijuana, in recent decades nearly all the
    59	states have
    60	changed their laws to permit the use of marijuana (or other cannabis products) for medical purposes.
    61	In
    62	addition, twenty-four states and the District of Columbia have passed laws removing certain state
    63	criminal
    64	prohibitions on recreational marijuana use by adults. As the Supreme Court has recognized, states
    65	cannot
    66	actually legalize marijuana because the states cannot change federal law, and the Constitution’s
    67	Supremacy Clause dictates that federal law takes precedence over conflicting state laws. So long as
    68	marijuana is a Schedule I controlled substance under the CSA, all unauthorized activities involving
    69	marijuana are federal crimes anywhere in the United States, including in states that have purported
    70	to
    71	legalize medical or recreational marijuana.
    72	Nonetheless, Congress has granted the states some leeway to allow the distribution and use of
    73	medical
    74	marijuana. In each budget cycle since FY2014, Congress has passed an appropriations rider barring
    75	the
    76	Department of Justice (DOJ) from using taxpayer funds to prevent states from “implementing their own
    77	laws that authorize the use, distribution, possession, or cultivation of medical marijuana.” Courts
    78	have
    79	interpreted the appropriations rider to prohibit federal prosecution of state-legal activities
    80	involving
    81	medical marijuana. However, it poses no bar to federal prosecution of activities involving
    82	recreational
    83	marijuana. Moreover, the rider does not remove criminal liability; it merely limits enforcement of
    84	the
    85	CSA in certain circumstances while the rider remains in effect. While official DOJ policy has varied
    86	somewhat across Administrations, recent presidential Administrations have not prioritized
    87	prosecution of
    88	state-legal activities involving marijuana.
    89	Even absent criminal prosecution or conviction, individuals and organizations engaged in
    90	marijuanarelated activities in violation of the CSA—including participants in the state-legal
    91	marijuana industry—
    92	may face collateral consequences arising from the federal prohibition of marijuana. Other federal
    93	laws
    94	impose legal consequences based on criminal activity, including violations of the CSA. For example,
    95	a
    96	financial institution handling income from a marijuana business may violate federal anti-money
    97	laundering laws. Likewise, Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code renders marijuana businesses
    98	ineligible for certain federal tax deductions. The presence of income from a marijuana-related
    99	business
   100	may also prevent a bankruptcy court from confirming a bankruptcy plan (though courts have split on
   101	the
   102	issue). For individuals, participation in the state-legal marijuana industry may have adverse
   103	immigration
   104	consequences. Violations of the CSA may also affect individuals’ ability to receive certain federal
   105	government benefits. In addition, federal law prohibits gun ownership and possession by any person
   106	who
   107	is an “unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance,” with no exception for users of
   108	state-legal
   109	medical marijuana.
   110	Legal Consequences If Marijuana Moved to Schedule III
   111	Moving marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III, without other legal changes, would not bring the
   112	state-legal medical or recreational marijuana industry into compliance with federal controlled
   113	substances
   114	law. With respect to medical marijuana, a key difference between placement in Schedule I and
   115	Schedule
   116	III is that substances in Schedule III have an accepted medical use and may lawfully be dispensed by
   117	Congressional Research Service 3
   118	prescription, while substances in Schedule I cannot. However, prescription drugs must be approved by
   119	the
   120	Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Although FDA has approved some drugs derived from or related

120	Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Although FDA has approved some drugs derived from or related
   121	to cannabis, marijuana itself is not an FDA-approved drug. Moreover, if one or more marijuana
   122	products
   123	obtained FDA approval, manufacturers and distributors would need to register with DEA and comply
   124	with
   125	regulatory requirements that apply to Schedule III substances in order to handle those products.
   126	Users of
   127	medical marijuana would need to obtain valid prescriptions for the substance from medical providers,
   128	subject to federal legal requirements that differ from existing state regulatory requirements for
   129	medical
   130	marijuana.
   131	Rescheduling marijuana would not affect the medical marijuana appropriations rider. Thus, so long as
   132	the
   133	current rider remains in effect, participants in the state-legal medical marijuana industry who
   134	comply with
   135	state law would be shielded from federal prosecution. If the rider were to lapse or be repealed,
   136	these
   137	persons would again be subject to prosecution at the discretion of DOJ.
   138	With respect to the manufacture, distribution, and possession of recreational marijuana, if
   139	marijuana were
   140	moved to Schedule III, such activities would remain illegal under federal law and potentially
   141	subject to
   142	federal prosecution regardless of their status under state law.
   143	Some criminal penalties for CSA violations depend on the schedule in which a substance is
   144	classified. If
   145	marijuana were moved to Schedule III, applicable penalties for some offenses would be reduced.
   146	However, CSA penalties that apply to activities involving marijuana specifically, such as the
   147	quantitybased mandatory minimum sentences discussed above, would not change as a result of
   148	rescheduling. DEA
   149	is not required to set annual production quotas for Schedule III controlled substances.
   150	The prohibition on business deductions in Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code applies to any
   151	trade
   152	or business that “consists of trafficking in controlled substances (within the meaning of schedule I
   153	and II
   154	of the Controlled Substances Act) which is prohibited by Federal law or the law of any State in
   155	which
   156	such trade or business is conducted.” Because the provision applies only to activities involving
   157	substances
   158	in Schedule I or II, moving marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III would allow marijuana
   159	businesses
   160	to deduct business expenses on federal tax filings. Other collateral legal consequences would
   161	continue to
   162	attach to unauthorized marijuana-related activities.
   163	Considerations for Congress
   164	Either Congress or the executive branch has the authority to change the status of marijuana under
   165	the
   166	CSA. Congress can change the status of a controlled substance through legislation, while the CSA
   167	empowers DEA to make scheduling decisions through the notice-and-comment rulemaking process.
   168	When considering whether to schedule or reschedule a controlled substance, DEA is bound by HHS’s
   169	recommendations on scientific and medical matters. However, DEA has stated that it has “final
   170	authority
   171	to schedule, reschedule, or deschedule a drug under the Controlled Substances Act.” A proposal from
   172	the
   173	118th Congress would provide for congressional review of DEA rescheduling decisions related to
   174	marijuana.
   175	If Congress wishes to change the legal status of marijuana, it has broad authority to do so before
   176	or after
   177	DEA makes any final scheduling decision. Several proposals from the 118th Congress would remove
   178	marijuana from control under the CSA or move the substance to a less restrictive schedule. If
   179	Congress
   180	moved marijuana to Schedule III by legislation, it could simultaneously consider whether to change
   181	some
   182	of the legal consequences of Schedule III status described above. Congress could also legislate to
   183	move
   184	marijuana to another CSA schedule, which would subject it to controls more or less stringent than
   185	those
   186	that apply to Schedule III controlled substances.
   187	Rescheduling or descheduling marijuana under the CSA could raise additional legal questions. For
   188	instance, FDA regulates certain cannabis products under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, so

   191	Congress might also consider whether to alter that regulatory regime or create some alternative
   192	regulatory
   193	framework. In addition, relaxing the CSA’s restrictions on marijuana could implicate the United
   194	States’
   195	international treaty obligations.
   196	While most recent proposals would relax federal regulation of marijuana, Congress could also seek to
   197	impose more stringent controls. One proposal from the 118th Congress would withhold certain federal

   199	is
